Leo and his grandfather had a special plan. They were going to build a wooden birdhouse together before spring arrived.

Grandpa carefully laid out the boards, a box of nails, and a small hammer on the workbench. "First we measure, then we cut, and then we build," he explained.

But Leo did not want to measure anything, because he wanted to start building right away. He grabbed two boards and began to hammer as fast as he could. The nails went in crooked, the roof slid off to one side, and the little door was too big.

Leo frowned at his work. "It looks like it is about to fall down," he said.

Grandpa smiled. "Lots of good things start out a little crooked," he said. "Shall we try again, slowly this time?"

So they tried again, and this time Leo held the ruler steady while Grandpa marked the wood with a pencil. They cut each board with care, and Leo tapped every nail in straight. The work took the whole afternoon.

When they were finished, the new birdhouse stood tall and even. They hung it on the maple tree beside the kitchen window.

Leo decided to keep the crooked birdhouse too, so he set it on a low branch just for fun.

A week later, Leo ran excitedly to find Grandpa. "Look!" he cried. A small brown wren was carrying twigs into the crooked birdhouse. Grandpa laughed and said, "I guess that bird likes your first try best."
stem: Why did Leo's first birdhouse come out crooked?
choices: Grandpa gave him the wrong nails.
The boards were too wet to use.
The hammer was too heavy for him.
He rushed and did not measure first.
explanation: Leo "did not want to measure anything, because he wanted to start building right away," so the nails went in crooked.

Rosa had been planning her lemonade stand for a whole week. She painted a sign with bright yellow letters, and she squeezed a big pitcher of lemons with her dad. Saturday was going to be perfect.

But on Saturday morning, Rosa woke up to the sound of rain tapping on her window. The sky was gray, and the air outside felt cold. Rosa pressed her nose against the glass and sighed.

"Nobody wants cold lemonade on a gloomy day like this," she said.

Her dad nodded slowly. "You may be right," he said. "So what do people want on a cold, rainy day?"

Rosa thought about it carefully. She remembered how she felt whenever she came inside after playing in the rain. Then she smiled. "They want something warm!" she said.

Together they made a big pot of hot cocoa. Rosa turned her sign over, and on the back she wrote HOT COCOA in big brown letters. She set up her table under the porch roof, where it would stay dry.

Soon a mail carrier stopped by, shaking the water off her hat. Then came a man walking his dog, and after him two children in rain boots. Each visitor held a warm cup in their cold hands and smiled.

By noon, the pot was completely empty. Rosa counted her coins and grinned. "Maybe rainy days are not so bad after all," she said.
stem: What problem does Rosa have at the start of the story?
choices: She cannot find any lemons to squeeze.
Her sign was lost before Saturday.
Her dad is too busy to help her.
It is cold and rainy on the day of her stand.
explanation: On Saturday morning Rosa "woke up to the sound of rain" and the air was cold, so she thinks no one will want lemonade.

passage:
Sea otters live in the chilly ocean waters along the coast of the North Pacific. Most sea animals have a thick layer of fat to keep them warm, but sea otters do not. Instead, they have the thickest fur of any animal on Earth. A patch of otter fur the size of a stamp has more hairs than a person has on a whole head! The fur traps tiny bubbles of air, and the air keeps the otter's skin warm and dry.

To keep their fur working well, sea otters spend hours each day cleaning it. They rub, comb, and fluff it with their paws, because a dirty coat would let in the cold water.

Sea otters must eat a lot of food to stay warm. They dive to the sea floor to find clams, crabs, and sea urchins. Some otters bring up a flat rock, too. They float on their backs and rest the rock on their bellies. Then they bang the shells against the rock until the shells crack open. Sea otters are one of the few animals that use tools.

When it is time to sleep, a sea otter does not want to drift away. So it wraps itself in long strands of kelp, a kind of seaweed that grows up from the ocean floor. The kelp works like an anchor and keeps the otter in place while it naps on the waves.
stem: What is this passage mainly about?
choices: why sea otters are the best swimmers in the sea
how kelp grows up from the ocean floor
why most sea animals have a thick layer of fat
how sea otters stay warm, eat, and rest in the ocean
explanation: Each paragraph describes a way otters live in the cold ocean: their fur, cleaning, finding food with tools, and sleeping in kelp.

Plants cannot walk, but their seeds can still go on long journeys. A seed that lands right under its parent plant may not grow well, because the big plant blocks the sunlight and drinks up most of the water. So plants have many clever ways to send their seeds far away.

Some seeds ride the wind. A dandelion seed has a puff of soft hairs, like a tiny umbrella, and when the wind blows, the seed floats away. Maple seeds have flat wings that spin like little helicopters as they fall.

Other seeds hitch a ride on animals. Burdock seeds are covered in small hooks that stick to the fur of a passing dog or deer. Later, the seeds fall off in a new place. Birds help too. They eat berries, and the seeds inside drop to the ground far away.

Some seeds travel by water. A coconut is a very large seed with a hard shell that keeps water out. It can float on the ocean for weeks and finally land on a faraway beach.

Wind, animals, and water all help plants spread out to new places. That way, each new plant can find its own space to grow.

choices: The ground under big plants is too hard.

explanation: The first paragraph says the big plant "blocks the sunlight and drinks up most of the water."

passage:
Wilson Bentley grew up on a farm in Vermont in the 1870s, where winters were long and snowy. Most people saw snow as cold, wet stuff to shovel. Wilson saw something different. He believed that every snowflake was a tiny work of art.

When Wilson was fifteen, his mother gave him an old microscope, and he used it to look at snowflakes up close. He tried to draw what he saw, but the flakes melted too quickly. He needed a better way.

Wilson wanted a special camera that could take pictures through a microscope. Such a camera cost a lot of money, but his parents helped him buy one. Then he spent two whole winters failing, because his pictures came out blurry or blank. Still, he did not give up. At last, on a January day in 1885, he took a clear photograph of a single snowflake. It was one of the first ever taken.

For the rest of his life, Wilson took pictures of snowflakes. He caught them on a black tray and moved them with a feather so they would not break. He took more than five thousand pictures, and he never found two flakes that were exactly alike.

Some neighbors laughed at the farmer who spent his days studying snow. Today, people call him "Snowflake Bentley," and scientists still study his photographs.
stem: Why did Wilson want a camera?
choices: His mother asked him to take photos of the farm.
His microscope was broken and needed a fix.
He wanted to sell pictures to his neighbors.
The snowflakes melted before he could draw them.
explanation: He "tried to draw what he saw, but the flakes melted too quickly," so he "needed a better way."

After the Rain

The rain has gone, the clouds have run,
and a puddle sits beside the sun.
It holds the sky and a tall green tree
and a smiling face that looks like me.

A robin hops down to take a sip,
and a leaf sails by like a tiny ship.
A beetle walking around the rim
stops and wonders if it should swim.

I jump right in, and the pictures shake!
The tree goes wiggly in my wake.
But if I stand still, I will soon see
the sky come back, and the tree, and me.

By noon the sun will drink it dry,
and I will have to find the sky
the old way, high above my head,
and not down at my feet instead.
stem: In the first stanza, when the puddle "holds the sky," it means the puddle
choices: is as large as the whole sky
has caught some falling rain
is hiding under a cloud
shows a reflection of the sky
explanation: The puddle also holds "a smiling face that looks like me," which shows it is reflecting what is above it like a mirror.

On the evening of my first piano recital, I wore shoes that pinched and a collar that itched, and I could not stop counting the rows of folding chairs in the auditorium. There were twelve rows, and I counted them four separate times while the younger students performed their short, bouncy songs.

My piece was a slow waltz that I had practiced every afternoon for three months. I had memorized it so completely that I could play it while thinking about something else entirely, which, my teacher warned me, was exactly the problem. "Knowing the notes with your fingers is not the same as knowing them with your head," Mrs. Okafor had told me. I had nodded politely, but I had not really been listening.

When my name was announced, I walked across the stage to the piano and sat down. The first page went smoothly, but halfway through the second page, my mind went completely blank. My fingers continued moving for a moment, the way your feet keep going after you miss a step on the stairs, and then they stopped.

The silence seemed to last for an hour, although it was probably about three seconds. I could hear someone's chair creak in the audience, and I could hear my own heartbeat. Then I remembered another piece of advice Mrs. Okafor used to give us: "If you get lost, don't go back. Find the next place you know and land there."

I skipped ahead to the final section, a passage I had practiced so many times that I could have hummed it in my sleep. My hands located the correct keys, and the waltz returned, a little shaky at first and then steady, and I played it all the way to the end.

Afterward, I expected Mrs. Okafor to be disappointed in me; instead, she shook my hand as if I were a grown-up. "Anyone can play a piece when nothing goes wrong," she said. "Tonight you learned how to keep going when something does."

I still get nervous before every performance, but now, along with the notes, I also practice the landing places.

Theo had been the strongest chess player in the after-school club for two consecutive years, so when Ms. Varga paired him with a third grader named June for the first match of the season, he almost felt sorry for her.

June was so small that she had to kneel on her chair to reach the far side of the board. She said very little, simply moving her pieces quietly, one after another, and recording each move in a spiral notebook with a purple pencil.

Theo played rapidly, the way he always did. He preferred to attack early, sending his knights and queen forward to put pressure on his opponent before the other player had settled in. Most of his opponents panicked and made careless mistakes, but June did not panic. Every time Theo threatened one of her pieces, she calmly moved it to safety or blocked the attack, and then she returned to strengthening her position, pawn by pawn.

By the twentieth move, Theo realized that his attack had run out of energy. His pieces were scattered across the board, while June's were organized like a sturdy wall. Ten moves later, she quietly announced, "Checkmate."

Theo stared at the board in disbelief, and he felt his face grow hot. For a moment, he wanted to explain that he had not really been trying, or that he was exhausted. Instead, he took a deep breath and asked, "Can you show me what you were doing?"

June's eyes lit up. She flipped open her notebook and walked him through the entire game, move by move, pointing out the exact moment when his queen had wandered too far from home. She explained that her grandfather had taught her to "build the house before you open the door."

That evening, Theo set up the board on his kitchen table and replayed the game twice. He was still the oldest player in the club. But for the first time in a long while, he felt like a beginner again, and to his surprise, he did not mind at all.

win the match against June easily
quit the chess club after this season
explanation: Theo is the club's strongest player and "almost felt sorry" for June, showing he expects an easy win.

passage:
If you scoop up a clump of damp moss and look at it under a microscope, you may find one of the toughest animals on the planet. It has eight stubby legs, each tipped with tiny claws, and it moves with a slow, rolling walk. Scientists call it a tardigrade, a name that means "slow stepper." Most people know it by its nickname: the water bear.

Water bears are tiny, usually less than a millimeter long, which is about the size of the period at the end of this sentence. They live almost everywhere: in moss and lichen, in soil, in the deep sea, and even on mountaintops. Yet what makes them remarkable is not where they live but what they can survive.

Like all animals, water bears need water to stay active. When their home dries out, however, they do not simply die. Instead, they pull in their legs, curl into a tight, dry ball called a tun, and let almost all the water leave their bodies. In this state, their metabolism, the set of chemical processes that keeps an animal alive, slows to nearly nothing. A water bear can stay as a tun for years. When water returns, it can swell back up and begin walking again within hours.

As tuns, water bears have survived conditions that would destroy most living things. In laboratory tests, they have lived through temperatures far below freezing, strong doses of radiation, and crushing pressure. In 2007, scientists even sent dried water bears into space on the outside of a satellite. Some of them survived the trip, and later they laid eggs that hatched into healthy young.

Researchers hope that studying water bears will lead to useful inventions. For example, scientists are studying the special proteins that protect a water bear's cells as they dry out. Someday, similar proteins might help keep medicines safe without a refrigerator.

explanation: The passage introduces the water bear and focuses on "what they can survive," including drying out, freezing, radiation, and space.

It has eight stubby legs, each tipped with tiny claws, and it moves with a slow, rolling walk. Scientists call it a tardigrade, a name that means "slow stepper." Most people know it by its nickname: the water bear.

Water bears are tiny, usually less than a millimeter long, which is about the size of the period at the end of this sentence. They live almost everywhere: in moss and lichen, in soil, in the deep sea, and even on mountaintops. Yet what makes them remarkable is not where they live but what they can survive.

Like all animals, water bears need water to stay active. When their home dries out, however, they do not simply die. Instead, they pull in their legs, curl into a tight, dry ball called a tun, and let almost all the water leave their bodies. In this state, their metabolism, the set of chemical processes that keeps an animal alive, slows to nearly nothing. A water bear can stay as a tun for years. When water returns, it can swell back up and begin walking again within hours.

As tuns, water bears have survived conditions that would destroy most living things. In laboratory tests, they have lived through temperatures far below freezing, strong doses of radiation, and crushing pressure. In 2007, scientists even sent dried water bears into space on the outside of a satellite. Some of them survived the trip, and later they laid eggs that hatched into healthy young.

Researchers hope that studying water bears will lead to useful inventions. For example, scientists are studying the special proteins that protect a water bear's cells as they dry out. Someday, similar proteins might help keep medicines safe without a refrigerator.

Every autumn, the forests of many northern regions seem to catch fire with color. Maples blaze orange and red, birches turn gold, and oaks fade to a deep rusty brown. It might seem as though the trees are painting their leaves for the season. In fact, much of the color was there all along.

During spring and summer, leaves are packed with a green pigment called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll absorbs sunlight and helps the tree turn water and carbon dioxide into sugar, the food it needs to grow. Because a leaf contains so much chlorophyll, its green color hides other pigments that are also present. Among these are carotenoids, the same yellow and orange pigments found in carrots and corn.

As the days grow shorter and the nights grow cooler, trees prepare for winter. They begin to seal off the connection between each leaf and its branch. Without fresh supplies, the chlorophyll breaks down and is not replaced. As the green fades, the yellows and oranges that were hidden underneath finally show through.

Reds and purples work differently. These colors come from pigments called anthocyanins, and most of them are not present in summer at all. Some trees make them in autumn, when sugars become trapped in the leaves. Bright, sunny days followed by cool nights tend to produce the most anthocyanins, which is why some autumns are especially vivid while others look dull.

Eventually, the leaves dry out and drop. This loss may look like a sad ending, but it is actually a clever survival strategy. Without its leaves, a tree loses far less water during the frozen months, when water in the ground is hard to reach. In spring, it will grow a fresh set, and the cycle will begin again.

explanation: The second and third paragraphs explain that carotenoids are present but hidden until "the yellows and oranges that were hidden underneath finally show through."

passage:
In the early 1800s, moving goods across the young United States was slow and expensive. Roads were rough dirt tracks that turned to mud in the rain, and wagons pulled by horses could carry only small loads. Shipping a ton of flour from Buffalo, on Lake Erie, to New York City could take weeks and cost far more than the flour itself was worth.

Some leaders proposed a bold solution: a canal, a human-made waterway, stretching more than 350 miles across New York State, from the Hudson River to Lake Erie. Many people thought the idea was foolish. The route crossed forests, swamps, and hills, and the nation had few trained engineers. Critics mockingly called the project "Clinton's Ditch," after the state's governor, who supported it.

Construction began in 1817. Thousands of workers, many of them recent immigrants, dug the channel largely by hand, using shovels, picks, and teams of horses and oxen. Because the land between the Hudson and Lake Erie rises by several hundred feet, the builders constructed locks, chambers with gates at each end that raise or lower boats from one water level to another. Along the way, the workers and their self-taught engineers invented new tools, such as a machine for pulling tree stumps out of the ground.

When the Erie Canal opened in 1825, it was an immediate success. Flat-bottomed boats, pulled by mules walking along a path beside the water, carried cargo across the state in a fraction of the old time. The cost of shipping fell by roughly ninety percent. Farmers in the Midwest could now sell their crops in eastern cities, and manufactured goods flowed west in return.

The canal changed the map of the nation. Towns along its route, such as Rochester and Syracuse, grew rapidly. New York City became the busiest port in the country. The "ditch" that critics had laughed at had become one of the most important building projects of its time.

passage:
When most people think of a library, they picture shelves of books and a quiet reading room. But a growing number of public libraries now lend out much more: sewing machines, telescopes, cake pans, garden tools, even musical instruments. These collections are sometimes called "libraries of things." I believe every community should have one.

The first reason is simple: many useful objects sit unused most of the time. A family might need a power drill for one afternoon to hang shelves, then leave it in a closet for a year. A ukulele might be played for a week before its owner loses interest. When a library owns these items, dozens of families can share a single one. Each household spends less money, and fewer objects end up in landfills.

Second, a library of things makes it easier to try something new. A child who is curious about the stars may not be able to afford a telescope. A grown-up who wants to learn to bake bread may not want to buy an expensive mixer before knowing whether baking is fun. Borrowing removes the risk. Just as a library book lets a reader explore a subject without buying a whole shelf, a borrowed tool lets a person explore a hobby without a large expense.

Some critics argue that libraries should stick to books and that lending objects is too costly or complicated. It is true that a telescope is harder to repair than a paperback. However, many libraries have found that the items last surprisingly well. Local businesses and volunteers often donate equipment or help with repairs. Besides, libraries have always changed with the times. They once lent only printed books; today they lend movies, audiobooks, and e-books. Lending objects is simply the next step.

At its heart, a library is built on a generous idea: that sharing makes a community richer. A library of things takes that idea and puts it into people's hands, quite literally. I hope that the next time you visit your library, you will be able to check out a book about birds and a pair of binoculars to go with it.

Ines lifted it out with both hands, as if it might still feel pain, and laid it on the felt-covered bench where Mr. Halloran performed his most meticulous restorations.

In the eleven months she had served as his apprentice, she had learned to sharpen chisels until they could shave a translucent curl from the end grain of spruce, to warm animal glue in a double boiler that smelled faintly of a barn, and, above all, to wait. Mr. Halloran did nothing hurriedly: he would examine a single crack for an entire morning before touching it, rotating the instrument beneath the lamp and running a fingertip along its edge as though deciphering a sentence written in a language only he understood.

When she finally asked whether it could be saved, he did not answer immediately; instead, he held the violin up to the window, and the afternoon light passed through the thin wood of the top, revealing a faint amber map of earlier repairs: a reinforcing cleat here, a patch there, the ghostly outline of a crack mended long before either of them was born.

"Look," he said, tracing the oldest of the patches with his finger. "Someone has already rescued it, three times, perhaps four. Whoever did this was not as careful as he might have been, but he was careful enough, and the violin kept singing."

Ines had expected him to criticize the earlier workmanship, as he frequently criticized hers. Instead, his voice contained something remarkably close to gratitude. It occurred to her that he was speaking not only of the violin's previous menders but also of himself, and perhaps of her as well: of all the imperfect hands an instrument passes through on its long journey from one century to the next.

They labored over the violin for six weeks, and Mr. Halloran permitted her to fit the new cleats along the split, small diamonds of spruce positioned crosswise to the grain, and he did not correct her once, although she noticed him look twice at the third one. "There," he said, handing the instrument to her with unexpected ceremony. "Now you are part of its history too."

That night, walking home through the darkening streets, Ines discovered that she was not thinking about the roughness at all. She was imagining some future apprentice, decades from now, holding the violin up to a window and discovering her small diamonds glowing in the light.

The Cartographer's Daughter

My father drew the coastlines of the world
from other people's journeys, never his:
the jagged inlets sailors had reported,
the islands rumored, half-imagined, named
for patrons who would never see them either.
He worked by lamplight, patient as the tide,
correcting capes by fractions of a degree.

I asked him once if it unsettled him
to chart a shoreline he could never verify.
He smiled and lifted up his finest pen.
"Each map," he said, "is someone's best belief,
recorded honestly, and then revised.
The world is always larger than the paper;
the error is in thinking we are finished."

Now, decades later, holding the exacting
photograph a satellite has taken,
I find his careful coastline wandering
a mile too far into the open water.
I do not mark it wrong; I trace it slowly,
the way one reads a treasured, faded letter,
and recognize the honesty of distance,
the faith of someone drawing what he was told
who left a margin for the truth to enter.

passage:
Every autumn, a small songbird called the European robin leaves its breeding grounds in Scandinavia and flies south toward the Mediterranean, often traveling at night and across unfamiliar terrain. Young birds making the journey for the first time have no experienced companions to follow. Yet they reliably head in the right direction. How they do this has puzzled biologists for more than a century.

Part of the answer, researchers now agree, is that many migratory birds can sense Earth's magnetic field. In the 1960s, German scientists placed robins in cages surrounded by electric coils that could alter the direction of the magnetic field. During the migratory season, the restless birds tended to hop toward one side of the cage. When the researchers rotated the magnetic field, the birds shifted their preferred direction accordingly. Intriguingly, the birds did not seem to respond to the field's polarity—whether it pointed north or south—but rather to its angle relative to the ground. In effect, they could tell "toward the pole" from "toward the equator." Scientists call this ability an inclination compass.

Detecting the field is one thing. Explaining how a living body does it is another. One leading hypothesis focuses on proteins called cryptochromes, located in the retina of the eye. According to this idea, when light strikes a cryptochrome molecule, it produces a pair of chemically reactive particles whose behavior is subtly influenced by the magnetic field. If this is correct, birds may literally see the field, perhaps as a faint pattern of light or shade overlaid on their ordinary vision. Supporting this view, experiments have shown that robins' magnetic sense is disrupted under certain colors of light and by weak radio-frequency noise, effects that would be difficult to explain if the sense depended solely on a magnetic mineral.

Still, the question is far from settled. Some birds appear to have tiny deposits of iron-containing minerals in their beaks or inner ears, and certain researchers suspect that these play a role as well, perhaps in measuring the strength of the field rather than its direction. It is entirely possible that birds use more than one magnetic mechanism, in addition to cues from the sun, the stars, and familiar landmarks.

What makes the subject especially compelling is that it lies at the boundary between biology and physics. If the cryptochrome hypothesis holds, it would mean that a phenomenon from quantum physics, usually observed only in carefully controlled laboratory conditions, is quietly operating inside a bird's eye, guiding it across a continent in darkness.

Every autumn, a small songbird called the European robin leaves its breeding grounds in Scandinavia and flies south toward the Mediterranean, often traveling at night and across unfamiliar terrain. Young birds making the journey for the first time have no experienced companions to follow. Yet they reliably head in the right direction. How they do this has puzzled biologists for more than a century.

Part of the answer, researchers now agree, is that many migratory birds can sense Earth's magnetic field. In the 1960s, German scientists placed robins in cages surrounded by electric coils that could alter the direction of the magnetic field. During the migratory season, the restless birds tended to hop toward one side of the cage. When the researchers rotated the magnetic field, the birds shifted their preferred direction accordingly. Intriguingly, the birds did not seem to respond to the field's polarity—whether it pointed north or south—but rather to its angle relative to the ground. In effect, they could tell "toward the pole" from "toward the equator." Scientists call this ability an inclination compass.

Detecting the field is one thing. Explaining how a living body does it is another. One leading hypothesis focuses on proteins called cryptochromes, located in the retina of the eye. According to this idea, when light strikes a cryptochrome molecule, it produces a pair of chemically reactive particles whose behavior is subtly influenced by the magnetic field. If this is correct, birds may literally see the field, perhaps as a faint pattern of light or shade overlaid on their ordinary vision. Supporting this view, experiments have shown that robins' magnetic sense is disrupted under certain colors of light and by weak radio-frequency noise, effects that would be difficult to explain if the sense depended solely on a magnetic mineral.

Still, the question is far from settled. Some birds appear to have tiny deposits of iron-containing minerals in their beaks or inner ears, and certain researchers suspect that these play a role as well, perhaps in measuring the strength of the field rather than its direction. It is entirely possible that birds use more than one magnetic mechanism, in addition to cues from the sun, the stars, and familiar landmarks.

What makes the subject especially compelling is that it lies at the boundary between biology and physics. If the cryptochrome hypothesis holds, it would mean that a phenomenon from quantum physics, usually observed only in carefully controlled laboratory conditions, is quietly operating inside a bird's eye, guiding it across a continent in darkness.

Most of us assume that more options are better. If a store offers twenty kinds of cereal rather than five, surely shoppers are more likely to find exactly what they want. Yet a well-known study published in 2000 suggested that, under some circumstances, abundance can be paralyzing.

In the study, psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting table at an upscale grocery store. On some days, the table displayed twenty-four varieties of gourmet jam; on other days, it displayed only six. Shoppers who stopped at the table received a coupon toward a purchase. The larger display attracted more visitors—about sixty percent of passersby stopped, compared with forty percent for the smaller one. But when the researchers tracked the coupons, the pattern reversed dramatically. Roughly thirty percent of the shoppers who saw six jams went on to buy one, while only about three percent of those who saw twenty-four did so.

The researchers proposed that a large set of options can create what came to be called "choice overload." Comparing many alternatives requires mental effort, and the more options there are, the more likely a person is to worry that a better choice was overlooked. Faced with this burden, some people simply decline to choose at all.

The jam study became famous, and the idea spread quickly into business books and popular articles. Later research, however, complicated the picture. When other scientists attempted to repeat similar experiments, they sometimes found the effect, sometimes found no effect, and occasionally found the opposite: larger assortments leading to more purchases. A broad review of dozens of studies concluded that the average effect of assortment size was close to zero.

This does not mean the original finding was mistaken. Instead, researchers have begun to identify the conditions under which choice overload is most likely to appear. It seems strongest when people do not already know what they prefer, when the options are difficult to compare, and when they feel pressure to make the best possible decision. A shopper who always buys strawberry jam will hardly be troubled by a shelf of two dozen flavors; a first-time buyer trying to select the perfect gift may be overwhelmed.

The history of the jam study offers a lesson that extends beyond psychology. A single striking result can capture the public imagination, but science advances by testing, questioning, and refining such results. The most useful conclusion is often not a simple rule—"more choice is bad"—but a more careful account of when, and for whom, a pattern holds.

The following letter is an imagined account, written in the style of the period, of a young woman's first railway journey in the early 1840s.

My dear Margaret,

You made me promise to write the moment I arrived, and so I sit, still in my traveling cloak, at Aunt Harriet's writing desk, my hand not altogether steady—though whether from the motion of the carriage or from sheer astonishment I cannot say.

I confess I approached the station this morning in a state of considerable dread. You will recall that Mr. Pell assured us at dinner last month that the human frame was never designed to travel at more than twenty miles in the hour, and that the rush of air at such velocities would certainly stop the breath. I half believed him, and when the engine came hissing alongside the platform, enormous and black and exhaling steam like some creature in a fable, I very nearly retreated to the coach office.

I did not retreat, and I am exceedingly glad of it. For the first few minutes I gripped the edge of the seat and kept my eyes fixed upon my gloves; but curiosity is a more powerful force than fear, at least in my temperament, and presently I looked out. Margaret, the fields went by as if someone were drawing a painted ribbon past the window. Hedges, cottages, a church tower, a boy waving from a gate—each appeared and vanished before I could properly take it in. My breath, I assure you, continued perfectly well, whatever Mr. Pell's predictions.

What struck me most was not the speed itself but what it does to distance. The journey that once cost Father two full days by coach, with a night at that miserable inn, I completed between breakfast and a late luncheon. It seems to me that the entire country has grown smaller since Tuesday. Aunt Harriet, who has lived her whole life in this town, says that the railway will bring London newspapers here on the very day they are printed, and that she hardly knows whether to be pleased or alarmed.

I confess I share something of her uncertainty. There is a great deal of soot, and the noise is beyond description, and I could not help but feel for the coachmen standing idle in the yard as we passed. Yet I cannot wish the thing undone, for I have seen the future arriving, and it came in at forty miles an hour.

Do tell Mother that I am entirely well, and that I wore my scarf exactly as she instructed; I shall write again on Sunday.

Your affectionate sister,
Eleanor

In recent years, boredom has become something most of us work hard to avoid. A few seconds of waiting—in line, at a bus stop, between classes—are enough to send many people reaching for a screen. The impulse is understandable: boredom is uncomfortable, and relief is always within reach. But I want to suggest that in eliminating boredom so efficiently, we may be surrendering something valuable.

Consider what boredom actually is. Psychologists often describe it as a signal: an unpleasant feeling that arises when our current activity fails to engage us. Like hunger, it is not pleasant, but it is useful. Hunger tells us to look for food; boredom tells us to look for something more meaningful to do. When we silence that signal the moment it appears, we lose its message. We trade the restless search for a new pursuit for a stream of small distractions that occupy our attention without ever satisfying it.

There is also evidence that boredom can nourish creativity. In one frequently cited experiment, participants who first completed a deliberately dull task—copying numbers from a telephone directory—later came up with more inventive uses for a pair of plastic cups than participants who skipped the tedious task. The researchers suggested that boredom prompts the mind to wander, and that a wandering mind is more likely to make unexpected connections. A single study cannot prove a general rule, of course, but the finding is consistent with the experience of many writers, scientists, and artists who report that their best ideas arrived during idle moments: on long walks, in the shower, while staring out a window.

Some will object that this argument romanticizes a feeling that, for many people, is simply miserable, and that chronic boredom is associated with poor concentration and unhappiness. This is a fair point. I am not arguing that boredom is pleasant or that it should be imposed on anyone as a kind of discipline. Prolonged, inescapable boredom—the kind experienced by someone trapped in meaningless work—is genuinely harmful. My claim is narrower: that brief, ordinary boredom, the kind we now dispel by reflex, deserves a little more tolerance.

What might that look like in practice? Perhaps it means leaving the phone in a pocket during a ten-minute wait, or allowing a free afternoon to remain unscheduled. It means treating the first flicker of restlessness not as a problem to be solved instantly but as an invitation. The mind, given a little empty space, has a way of filling it with something of its own making. We should be willing, now and then, to find out what.

In recent years, boredom has become something most of us work hard to avoid. A few seconds of waiting—in line, at a bus stop, between classes—are enough to send many people reaching for a screen. The impulse is understandable: boredom is uncomfortable, and relief is always within reach. But I want to suggest that in eliminating boredom so efficiently, we may be surrendering something valuable.

Consider what boredom actually is. Psychologists often describe it as a signal: an unpleasant feeling that arises when our current activity fails to engage us. Like hunger, it is not pleasant, but it is useful. Hunger tells us to look for food; boredom tells us to look for something more meaningful to do. When we silence that signal the moment it appears, we lose its message. We trade the restless search for a new pursuit for a stream of small distractions that occupy our attention without ever satisfying it.

There is also evidence that boredom can nourish creativity. In one frequently cited experiment, participants who first completed a deliberately dull task—copying numbers from a telephone directory—later came up with more inventive uses for a pair of plastic cups than participants who skipped the tedious task. The researchers suggested that boredom prompts the mind to wander, and that a wandering mind is more likely to make unexpected connections. A single study cannot prove a general rule, of course, but the finding is consistent with the experience of many writers, scientists, and artists who report that their best ideas arrived during idle moments: on long walks, in the shower, while staring out a window.

Some will object that this argument romanticizes a feeling that, for many people, is simply miserable, and that chronic boredom is associated with poor concentration and unhappiness. This is a fair point. I am not arguing that boredom is pleasant or that it should be imposed on anyone as a kind of discipline. Prolonged, inescapable boredom—the kind experienced by someone trapped in meaningless work—is genuinely harmful. My claim is narrower: that brief, ordinary boredom, the kind we now dispel by reflex, deserves a little more tolerance.

What might that look like in practice? Perhaps it means leaving the phone in a pocket during a ten-minute wait, or allowing a free afternoon to remain unscheduled. It means treating the first flicker of restlessness not as a problem to be solved instantly but as an invitation. The mind, given a little empty space, has a way of filling it with something of its own making. We should be willing, now and then, to find out what.
